title: What is Latency?
summary: Latency is the total time delay incurred for data packets to travel from a source endpoint to a destination across a network, measured in milliseconds.

body.definition: The elapsed time between the transmission of a data frame and its successful receipt at the remote destination, often expressed as Round-Trip Time (RTT).

body.text: Latency is bounded by the physical speed of light through fiber optics (~200,000 km/s in glass), intermediate routing hops, packet queue serialization, and server processing overhead. Even on a gigabit connection, a packet crossing oceans takes tens of milliseconds due to physical distance.
Sources of Latency

items: Propagation Delay: Time for electromagnetic signals to travel along physical media.
Serialization Delay: Time required to clock packet bits onto the physical wire.
Queuing Delay: Time packets wait in router buffer queues during network congestion (bufferbloat).
Processing Delay: Time routers take to examine packet headers and determine route tables.

body.text: Ping measures RTT (Round Trip Time). A 20ms ping means it takes 10ms for your packet to reach the host and 10ms for the echo reply to return.

title: Network Bandwidth
summary: Bandwidth is the maximum theoretical volume of digital information that a transmission medium or channel can transfer per unit of time.

body.definition: The maximum data transfer capacity of a network link or communication channel, measured in bits per second (e.g. Mbps, Gbps).

body.text: Bandwidth is like the diameter of a water pipe: a wider pipe allows more volume of water to pass through simultaneously, but does not increase the speed of the water itself. High bandwidth allows many concurrent data streams without bottlenecking.
Bits vs Bytes: The 8x Difference

Internet Service Providers advertise bandwidth in megabits per second (Mbps), while file downloads are displayed in megabytes per second (MB/s). Because 1 Byte = 8 bits, a 100 Mbps internet connection yields a theoretical maximum download rate of 12.5 MB/s.
Bandwidth dictates capacity, whereas latency dictates delay. High bandwidth with high latency is suitable for bulk file transfers, but terrible for real-time multiplayer gaming or VoIP.

title: Network Throughput
summary: Throughput is the actual, measured quantity of successful payload data delivered across a network connection in real-world operating conditions.

body.definition: The rate at which usable application data is successfully transmitted over a network channel after subtracting protocol overhead, packet loss, and retransmissions.

body.text: While bandwidth represents the ideal theoretical ceiling, throughput is what your applications actually achieve. Factors like TCP window scaling, encryption overhead (TLS/IPsec), packet loss, and electromagnetic interference on Wi-Fi reduce actual throughput below maximum bandwidth.
Goodput vs Throughput
Throughput includes transport and IP protocol header overhead as well as duplicate retransmissions. Goodput measures exclusively the application payload bytes delivered to the end process.
According to the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP = Bandwidth x RTT), achieving maximum throughput over high-latency links requires sufficiently large TCP receive buffer windows.

title: Domain Name System (DNS)
summary: DNS is the decentralized naming system that translates human-readable domain names like example.com into machine-routable IP addresses.

body.definition: A hierarchical distributed database system that maps hostnames to IP addresses, mail exchange records, and cryptographic public keys.

body.text: When you enter a web address into a browser, your system queries a recursive resolver (like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8), which navigates the root nameservers, TLD nameservers (.com), and authoritative nameservers to fetch the matching A or AAAA records.
Resolution Hierarchy

items: Root Zone: 13 named root authority server clusters coordinating top-level delegations.
Top-Level Domain (TLD): Servers handling extensions like .com, .org, or country codes.
Authoritative Nameserver: The final server holding the actual domain zone records.
Time-To-Live (TTL): A cache duration indicator dictating how long resolvers may store answers.

body.text: Modern privacy protocols like DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt DNS lookups, preventing ISPs from observing which domains you query.

title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
summary: NAT maps entire private local networks to a single public IP address by translating port numbers in IP packet headers at the router boundary.

body.definition: A method that modifies network address information in IP packet headers while in transit across a routing device, multiplexing private IPs over public IPs.

body.text: Because IPv4 addresses are limited (only ~4.3 billion exist), home and corporate routers assign devices private IPs (such as 192.168.1.x or 10.x.x.x). When your phone requests a website, the router replaces the local private IP and port with its own public IP and a unique source port, maintaining a translation table to route the reply back.
NAT Types in Consumer Routers

rows.label: Type 2 (Moderate / Port-Restricted)
values: Standard NAT with UPnP / port forwarding

rows.label: Type 3 (Strict / Symmetric NAT)
values: Dynamic random port mapping per destination

body.text: Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) places an additional layer of NAT at the ISP level, making port forwarding impossible without public IPv6 or tunneling.

title: TCP vs UDP Protocols
summary: TCP guarantees reliable, ordered packet delivery via handshakes, whereas UDP prioritizes minimal latency with connectionless, unordered transmission.

body.definition: A connection-oriented transport protocol that ensures reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of a stream of octets between applications.

body.text: TCP establishes connections using a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). It numbers each packet, sends acknowledgments for received segments, and retransmits lost packets. This makes it ideal for web pages, APIs, and file downloads where every byte must arrive intact.
User Datagram Protocol (UDP)

UDP is connectionless. It fires packets (datagrams) toward the destination with zero handshaking, zero acknowledgment, and zero ordering guarantees. If a packet drops, it is ignored. This zero-overhead architecture makes UDP essential for live video streams, voice calls, and real-time gaming.
QUIC and HTTP/3 run on top of UDP, implementing modern reliability, congestion control, and TLS encryption in userspace without TCP head-of-line blocking.

title: Content Delivery Networks (CDN)
summary: A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that cache content physically close to end users to slash latency.

body.definition: A globally distributed cluster of edge caching servers that serve cached static and dynamic web assets from points of presence nearest to the requesting client.

body.text: Without a CDN, a user in Tokyo requesting assets from an origin server in Frankfurt suffers ~250ms round-trip latency on every asset. A CDN edge server in Tokyo caches the images, CSS, and API responses, returning them in under 10ms over local peering links.
Edge Caching & Anycast Routing

CDNs use BGP Anycast routing so that a single IP address directs incoming traffic to the topologically closest healthy edge point-of-presence (PoP), mitigating DDoS attacks while load balancing traffic.
CDNs do not merely cache images: modern Edge compute workers allow executing JavaScript / WebAssembly logic directly at the edge before hitting origin databases.
